encounters.cc: Chronic epigastric discomfort and unintentional weight loss

lines: Chronic epigastric discomfort and unintentional weight loss
He describes the pain as dull and non-radiating, worsening after meals, and often accompanied by bloating and greasy, foul-smelling stools.
He has no history of blood in stool, vomiting, or fevers.
His past medical history is notable for multiple prior hospitalizations for acute pancreatitis, most recently eight months ago.
He is not taking any regular medications and denies NSAID use.
He drinks six to eight beers daily and smokes one pack of cigarettes per day.
On exam, he appears thin but in no distress.
There is mild epigastric tenderness without rebound or guarding.
Laboratory testing reveals a normal serum calcium and lipase.
Stool analysis is positive for fat and undigested muscle fibers.
D-xylose test results are within normal limits.
A CT scan of the abdomen is performed and shown below.

encounters.cc: Routine check-up and lung cancer screening inquiry

lines: Routine check-up and lung cancer screening inquiry
This 57-year-old male with hypertension and chronic pancreatitis returns following his Gastroenterology evaluation.
He has no complaints but is concerned about his risk for lung cancer due to his 30-pack-year smoking history.
He inquires about lung cancer screening.
Discussed the option of low-dose computed tomography (LDCT) and explained the importance of understanding the trade-offs between sensitivity and specificity when interpreting screening results.
Mentioned a new blood biomarker test for lung cancer that is under consideration.
The receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve for this test shows that at a cutoff value of 50 units, the sensitivity is 90% and the specificity is 70%.
If the cutoff value is increased to 70 units, the sensitivity decreases to 75%, but the specificity increases to 85%.
The patient asks which cutoff value would be more appropriate for him, considering his risk factors.

encounters.cc: Progressive difficulty walking with calf and buttock pain

lines: Progressive difficulty walking with calf and buttock pain

The patient is a 58-year-old male with hypertension and chronic pancreatitis previously seen in Gastroenterology and Internal Medicine who presents with progressive difficulty walking over the past year.
He reports that after walking about 200 meters, he develops cramping pain in his calves and buttocks that resolves with rest.
Recently, he has also noticed erectile dysfunction that has become persistent.
He has a history of poorly controlled hypertension.
He denies trauma, fever, or recent infection.
On examination, the patient has diminished femoral pulses bilaterally, and dorsalis pedis pulses are not palpable.
The lower extremities are cool to touch with sparse hair distribution.
Neurologic exam shows intact strength and sensation in both legs.
Cardiac exam reveals no murmurs, and lung auscultation is clear.
Laboratory studies show normal renal function and hemoglobin A1c.

encounters.cc: Persistent left-sided ear pain for 6 weeks

lines: Persistent left-sided ear pain for 6 weeks
This patient with hypertension, chronic pancreatitis, and Leriche syndrome presents with ear pain.
He reports that the pain is dull and constant, and it occasionally radiates to the throat.
He denies hearing loss, tinnitus, or discharge from the ear.
The patient has a 40-pack-year smoking history and consumes alcohol daily.
His vital signs are within normal limits.
On examination, the left ear appears normal with an intact tympanic membrane and no signs of inflammation or infection.
However, palpation of the neck reveals a firm, non-tender lymph node in the left cervical chain.
The patient's voice is hoarse, which he attributes to "just a bad habit of clearing my throat." He has no respiratory distress or stridor.
- Complete blood count: Within normal limits
- Basic metabolic panel: Within normal limits

encounters.cc: Persistent sore throat with 10-pound unintentional weight loss

lines: Persistent sore throat with 10-pound unintentional weight loss

The patient with chronic pancreatitis and prior ENT cancers returns with sore throat for the past 8 weeks, denying recent upper respiratory infections but reporting 10-pound unintentional weight loss over the last two months.
- Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (diagnosed 2022-01-15)
He has no history of alcohol abuse or exposure to human papillomavirus.
His vital signs are within normal limits.
On examination, you note a 2 cm ulcerative lesion on the right tonsil with ipsilateral cervical lymphadenopathy.
The patient has a hoarse voice and no apparent lesions on the oral mucosa or tongue.
- Complete Blood Count (CBC): Within normal limits
A biopsy of the tonsillar lesion is performed.

encounters.cc: Epigastric pain radiating to back with new-onset diabetes and weight loss

lines: Epigastric pain radiating to back with new-onset diabetes and weight loss

The patient, with a known history of chronic pancreatitis and prior head and neck malignancies, presents to the clinic with a 3-month history of epigastric pain radiating to the back, unexplained weight loss, and new-onset diabetes mellitus.
He denies any recent trauma or bleeding episodes.
- Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (diagnosed 2022-01-15)
- Squamous cell carcinoma of the tonsil (diagnosed 2023-01-15)
His past medical history is significant for chronic pancreatitis and a 20-pack-year smoking history.
Smoking: Current smoker, 40 pack-year history (approximately 1 pack per day since age 17).
Alcohol: Heavy daily alcohol consumption (6-8 beers per day).
On physical examination, he appears jaundiced with scleral icterus.
An abdominal examination reveals a palpable, nontender gallbladder.
- Activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT): 30 seconds (normal: 25-35 seconds)
An abdominal CT scan shows a mass in the head of the pancreas with liver metastases.

encounters.cc: Sudden onset severe tearing back pain with leg weakness and difficulty urinating

lines: Sudden onset severe tearing back pain with leg weakness and difficulty urinating
This patient with hypertension, chronic pancreatitis, and pancreatic cancer presents with back pain that began several hours ago.
The pain is described as tearing and radiates to his abdomen.
He also reports difficulty urinating and weakness in both legs.
- Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (diagnosed 2022-01-15)
- Squamous cell carcinoma of the tonsil (diagnosed 2023-01-15)
- Pancreatic adenocarcinoma (mucin-producing) with chronic disseminated intravascular coagulation (diagnosed 2024-01-15)
On physical examination, his blood pressure is 180/95 mmHg, heart rate is 88 beats per minute, and he is afebrile.
Neurological examination reveals decreased strength in the lower extremities, more pronounced in the flexor groups, and loss of pain and temperature sensation over the trunk and legs.
Light touch and proprioception are intact.
The patient has a flaccid bladder and decreased rectal tone.
An urgent CT angiography of the chest and abdomen is performed, revealing a descending thoracic aortic dissection extending to the level of T10.
